GRADE 2 · PIANOS / SOUND & MOTION

The note inside.

Where does a piano's note come from?

FOUR LITTLE WONDERS

Where shall we look?

Choose a question with your grown-up. Look for a clue in the picture before you open the explanation.

01Where could a note be hiding?↗02How can a string keep singing after one tap?↗03How does a thin string fill a room with sound?↗04Why do the two ends of a piano sound different?↗

Grown-up beside you. A question is enough.

LOOK TOGETHER · 01

Where could a note be hiding?

Find Little's hand and the orange arrow. One key moves only a little. Where would you look for what happens next?

A little explanation & something to try

The piano is not a box of stored notes. Pressing a key starts moving parts inside. In an acoustic piano, those parts send a small hammer toward metal strings. The next picture lets us look at a model of that hidden motion.

Try together. Pretend the tabletop is a piano key. Lower one finger quietly, then lift it. Tell your grown-up what you imagine moving inside.

LOOK TOGETHER · 02

How can a string keep singing after one tap?

Find the gap between the hammer and the string. Look for the two faint orange traces. What might they help us imagine?

A little explanation & something to try

A hammer taps the string and falls away. The string keeps moving back and forth very quickly. That motion is vibration. The orange traces exaggerate the movement; they are not extra strings. The vibration gradually fades unless something stops it sooner.

Try together. Move one finger a tiny distance back and forth in the air. Let it become still. Say when your pretend string could make sound.

LOOK TOGETHER · 03

How does a thin string fill a room with sound?

Find the narrow raised bridge and the broad wooden board. Where do the strings meet the bridge? Follow the orange mark into the wood.

A little explanation & something to try

A thin string alone moves little air. Its vibration passes through the bridge into the soundboard. This broad wooden board vibrates too, moving more air. The moving air carries sound to our ears. The wood helps us hear a small string's motion.

Try together. Trace the path with your finger: string, bridge, soundboard. Finish by pointing toward your ear. What helped the motion reach you?

LOOK TOGETHER · 04

Why do the two ends of a piano sound different?

The display has two strings. Trace each from one support to the other. What is different about the distance between the supports?

A little explanation & something to try

Pitch means how high or low a note sounds. With other things the same, a longer string gives a lower pitch and a shorter one gives a higher pitch. Tightening the same string raises its pitch; loosening it lowers the pitch. In a piano, length, thickness, and tension work together. Low notes are toward the player's left; high notes are toward the right.

Try together. Use your voice to make a comfortable low hum, then a higher hum. Keep both gentle. Can a high sound be quiet too?

A STORY TO OPEN TOGETHER

The note inside.

One key moves. A note rings out. Little follows it inside.

One little page at a time.

One small press

One small press

One key sinks beneath Little's hand. A note rings through the museum. “Was it hiding in there?” Little asks. Big listens beside the bench. The key hardly moved. Something inside the piano must have done much more.

What would you look for inside? Keep your guess for the next picture.

A hidden tap

A hidden tap

An enormous model gives them a peek. A key tips; connected parts lift a felt-covered hammer. Tap! The hammer strikes a string and comes away. “A tiny hammer?” Little whispers. This team of moving parts is called the action.

Follow the model from key to hammer. Why might the hammer need to come away?

After the tap

After the tap

The hammer has fallen back, but the string is not still. It quivers: back and forth, back and forth. That quick motion is vibration. “The tap is over,” Little says, “but the moving isn't!” How can such a thin string sound so big?

Find the gap. What keeps moving after the hammer's tap?

The wood joins in

The wood joins in

Little follows a string to a wooden bridge. The bridge carries vibration into a broad soundboard. That wood vibrates too, moving more air. The air carries sound to listening ears. “The wood joins in!” Little says. A thin string has a roomy helper.

Trace the connection into the wood. What does the soundboard help move?

Two lengths to notice

Two lengths to notice

Two strings stretch across another model. One is longer. If everything else stays the same, the longer string vibrates more slowly and sounds lower. The shorter one sounds higher. “Different voices!” says Little. How high or low a note sounds is its pitch.

Point to the string you predict would sound lower. What must stay the same for this comparison?

Keep the path

Keep the path

With the pedal up, Little releases a middle key. A felt damper hushes its strings. Little sketches key, hammer, strings, wood. “The note wasn't hiding. We set things moving!” Big leaves room for one more why.

What changed Little's first guess? What connection could you add to the sketch?

A note for your grown-up

Small discoveries. Time together.

For grown-ups & print downloads

Wonder first; explanations can wait. This is an acoustic piano; digital pianos usually make sound electronically through speakers. Museum models omit parts and exaggerate motion. They are not building plans or exact key/string counts. The action lets the hammer rebound while a key stays down. The bridge carries string vibration into the soundboard, which moves more air using energy from the strike. Pitch depends on vibration rate; loudness depends largely on vibration size. Compare string lengths with material, thickness, and tension unchanged: longer gives lower pitch; shorter gives higher. For the same string and vibrating length, tighter gives higher and looser gives lower. Real pianos combine length, thickness, and tension; low strings are longer and heavier. Pressing harder mainly changes loudness. Many notes use two or three strings. With the sustain pedal up, dampers return as keys are released; the highest strings often lack dampers. The story uses a middle key. Add the missing bridge or air to Little's sketch. Pictures, gentle humming, talking, and drawing are enough. Do not open a piano, touch or tighten strings, or build these models. Welcome dictation and stop whenever you have had enough.

About 15 min: share the six short scenes, then revisit a picture. Read aloud for Leo; pointing, talking, and pausing count. Let Little's first guess hang in the air before following the clues. The foldable carries the same story.
